title: Resource Use and Sustainability
summary: Renewable and non-renewable resources, sustainable use, water, soil and energy resources in South Africa, and how communities and governments can manage resources wisely.

notes.text: Something found in nature that people use to meet their needs, such as water, soil, forests, fish, minerals and sunlight.

rows: Can be replaced naturally within a human lifetime if used carefully
Cannot be replaced once used up, or take millions of years to form
Sunlight, wind, water, forests, fish, soil (if conserved)
Coal, oil, natural gas, gold, platinum, iron ore

notes.text: Development that meets the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

South Africa is a **water-scarce** country: its average rainfall (about 450 mm a year) is little more than half the world average, and rainfall is uneven, with the west much drier than the east. Most water is used by **agriculture (irrigation)**, followed by towns and industries.

items: **Threats**: droughts (e.g. the Cape Town 'Day Zero' crisis of 2017–2018), pollution from sewage, mines and factories, alien plants that use large amounts of water, and leaking pipes.

**Solutions**: fixing leaks, water restrictions, rainwater tanks, grey-water reuse, drip irrigation, removing alien plants (the **Working for Water** programme), desalination and inter-basin transfers such as the **Lesotho Highlands Water Project**.

notes.text: Only about **12%** of South Africa's land is suitable for growing crops. Fertile soil takes hundreds of years to form but can be lost quickly through **soil erosion**, caused by overgrazing, ploughing slopes, removing vegetation and poor farming.

About 80% of South Africa's electricity comes from **coal**, which is non-renewable and causes air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Load-shedding has shown how important it is to diversify. South Africa has excellent conditions for **solar** (in the Northern Cape) and **wind** energy (along the coasts).

rows: Overfishing of species such as abalone and snoek
Fishing quotas, closed seasons, marine protected areas
Overgrazing leads to soil erosion and desertification
Cutting trees for firewood; harvesting medicinal plants

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: Remember the three Rs: **Reduce** (use less), **Reuse** (use again), **Recycle** (turn waste into new products). Each one saves resources and reduces pollution.

**Community-based conservation** gives local people a share in the benefits of protecting resources, for example jobs and income from eco-tourism in game reserves such as the Makuleke region of the Kruger National Park.
